## Part 1 — Set Up Your Tools {background-color="#1A1A1A"}

Positron · Quarto · Antigravity 2.0 · Claude Desktop · GitHub · Git

## Install Positron

::: {.goal}
Positron is a free program from Posit where you write and run R code.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Install **R** first (4.2 or newer) from cran.r-project.org
- Then install **Positron** from positron.posit.co
- **File → Open Folder** opens your project
- **Ctrl + Enter** runs the current line
- No Positron? **Posit Cloud** runs the same code online
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](images/screenshots/01-positron.jpg){fig-alt="Positron with the fbs-analysis project open: files on the left, an R script in the editor, and the R console, variables and plots panes on the right." width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Quarto: Code and Words in One File

::: {.goal}
Quarto turns one file of words and code into a report, a Word document or slides.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- A `.qmd` file holds a YAML header, your text and code cells
- **Render** runs the code and builds HTML, Word, PDF or slides
- Quarto comes with Positron, so there is nothing extra to install
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](images/screenshots/04-quarto-positron.jpg){fig-alt="A Quarto file open in Positron, showing the YAML header at the top, a section heading and an R code cell below it." width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Quarto: The YAML Header and Structure

::: {.goal}
The YAML header at the top tells Quarto what to make.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
````markdown
---
title: "Fasting Blood Sugar Analysis"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---

## Read the data

```{{r}}
library(readxl)
fbs <- read_excel("datasets/mssm_fbs_workshop.xlsx")
```
````
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Between the two `---` lines is the YAML: one `key: value` per line
- `##` starts a section; plain text is your explanation
- A code cell runs R and puts its result in the report
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Change `format: html` to `format: docx` and render again: the same file becomes a Word document.
:::

## Install Claude Desktop (Optional)

::: {.goal}
Claude Desktop runs Claude Code in a window, so you do not need the terminal.
:::

- Download from claude.ai/download for Windows or macOS
- Sign in with your Claude account; Claude Code needs a paid plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise)
- The app has three tabs: **Chat**, **Cowork** and **Code**
- **Code** tab → **Local** → **Select folder** opens your project
- No paid plan? Skip this slide; Antigravity 2.0 is enough for today

::: {.note}
Claude Code includes everything it needs, so there is no terminal or extra install.
:::

## GitHub Account and First Repository

::: {.goal}
GitHub keeps your code online, with a full history of every change.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Sign up at github.com/signup with an email you will keep
- Verify your email before anything else
- Click **+** → **New repository**; name it, e.g. `fbs-analysis`
- **Private** while you work; Public when you publish
- Click **Create repository**
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](images/screenshots/02-github-new-repo.jpg){fig-alt="A new, empty GitHub repository page showing the repository address and the commands to push a project to it." width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Install and Check Git

::: {.goal}
Git records every change to your files on your computer. GitHub keeps a copy online.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Windows: install **Git for Windows** from git-scm.com/install/windows and accept the default options
- It brings **Git Credential Manager**, which signs you in to GitHub through your browser
- macOS: type `git --version`; if Git is missing, macOS offers to install it
- Check in a terminal, the window where you type commands (Positron: **Terminal → New Terminal**)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```bash
git --version
# git version 2.56.0.windows.2

git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Use the same email as your GitHub account, so your commits are linked to you.
:::

::: {.notes}
Git and GitHub are not the same thing. Git is a free program on your own
computer that saves snapshots of your project; GitHub is a website that keeps
a copy of those snapshots online. The two `git config` lines are typed once per
computer and tell Git who you are; every commit you make carries this name and
email. Any recent version number from `git --version` is fine. If it says the command is not found on Windows, close and
reopen Positron or Antigravity after installing, because a terminal opened
before the install does not know about Git yet.
:::

## Personal Access Token: a Password for Git

::: {.goal}
A personal access token (PAT) is a long password that GitHub makes for Git. Most of you will not need one today.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**When it is useful**

- The browser sign-in from Git Credential Manager fails or never appears
- You work without that sign-in, e.g. Posit Cloud or R packages such as `usethis`
- Git asks for a password: paste the token, never your GitHub password
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**How to make a classic token**

- GitHub: **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) → Generate new token (classic)**
- Tick the **repo** scope, set an expiry such as 30 days, and copy it: GitHub shows it only once
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Treat a token like a password. Never paste it into an AI prompt, a `.qmd` file or a commit.
:::

::: {.notes}
A classic token with the repo scope can read and change every repository you
own, which is why it should expire. When it expires, make a new one the same
way. In R, `usethis::create_github_token()` opens the same GitHub page with the
scopes already ticked, and `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()` asks for the token and
stores it safely, so you paste it once. If a token ever appears in a file you
pushed, delete the token on GitHub straight away and make a new one; deleting
the file is not enough, because the old commit still holds it.
:::

## Prompt Your Assistant to Commit and Push

::: {.goal}
Tell the assistant in plain words what to save and where to send it. It types the Git commands for you.
:::

```text
Render fbs-report.qmd to HTML. Then commit fbs-report.qmd and
fbs-report.html with the message "Add first FBS report" and push to GitHub.
```

- **Commit**: save a snapshot of your files, with a short message saying what changed
- **Push**: send your commits from your computer to your repository on GitHub
- Name the files, the commit message and where to push; a vague prompt gets a vague result
- Read the commands the assistant runs, then refresh your repository page on github.com

::: {.notes}
The rendered HTML file is the report other people can open without R, so it
is worth pushing next to the `.qmd` that made it. Antigravity may ask you to
approve each command before it runs; read the command and accept it only if it
matches what you asked for. The data file in `datasets/` is never pushed: it
is listed in `.gitignore`, which you set up in the hands-on in Part 4.
:::

## Check: Antigravity and GitHub Work Together

::: {.goal}
One small test push proves that Git, your GitHub sign-in and Antigravity all work.
:::

- Antigravity is open, you are signed in, and it answers a simple question
- Prompt: *Clone github.com/your-username/fbs-analysis into my Documents folder*, then open that folder
- Prompt: *Create README.md with one line, "My FBS analysis", then commit and push it*
- If a GitHub sign-in window opens, sign in; use a token only if that fails
- Refresh your repository on github.com: README.md is there

::: {.note}
Stuck at any line? Raise your hand now. Part 4 ends with a push, so this must work.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clone means making a copy of a GitHub repository on your computer, linked to
it so that later pushes go back to the same place. Replace your-username with
your own GitHub username; the repository is the one you made on the GitHub
slide. Common problems: Git is not installed, so the clone fails at once; the
browser sign-in was closed, so the push is refused; or the user.name and
user.email lines were skipped, so the commit is refused. Fix the one that
matches the message and ask Antigravity to try again.
:::

## Ready to Start: a Checklist

::: {.goal}
Tick all five before Part 2. Ask for help now, not during the hands-on.
:::

- Positron opens your project folder, and `1 + 1` runs in the Console
- A new `.qmd` file renders to HTML in Positron
- Antigravity 2.0 is installed and you are signed in
- Git is installed, and your test README push shows on github.com
- Optional: Claude Desktop opens your folder in the Code tab
